newsitem.title: INDIA: India eases state control on 5 industries, 9 firms.
newsitem.headline: India eases state control on 5 industries, 9 firms.

text.p: India took a big step ahead in its economic reform programme on Friday, ending state permission for manufacturing in five industries and slashing political and bureaucratic controls on nine large state-run companies.

"Today, the cabinet has de-licensed five items from the purview of the Industrial Development and Regulation Act," Industry Minister Murasoli Maran told a news conference, two days before leaving on an investment-shopping tour to Britain.

The five industries, in which aspiring manufacturers will no longer require prior government licence, are animal fats and oils; tanned or dressed fur skins; asbestos; paper and newsprint (barring bagasse-based units); and plywood and similar wood products.

Nine chosen profit-making state firms, including leaders in oil, petroleum and telecommunications, would have more autonomy to raise debt at home and abroad, establish joint ventures and incur capital expenses without monetary ceilings, Maran said.
"It is intended that these "navratnas" (nine jewels) should become truly world class entities," the Industry Ministry said in a statement.

"The strategy for this aims at turning them into autonomous board-managed companies, with minimal requirement of approaching the government for approvals," it said. The nine firms were expected to make "vision statements" within 90 days, it added.
The firms would be restructured with outside help from eminent non-official directors, it said.

In 1991, India began a sweeping reform programme to end decades-old socialist licence controls. Only nine industries still remain under licence control. Among them are coal, sugar, petroleum, cigarettes and pharmaceuticals.

The nine companies given more autonomy were Bharat Heavy Electricals Ltd, Bharat Petroleum Corp Ltd, Hindustan Petroleum Corp Ltd, Indian Oil Corp Ltd, Indian Petrochemicals Corp Ltd, National Thermal Power Corp, Oil and Natural Gas Corp, Steel Authority of India Ltd and Videsh Sanchar Nigam Ltd.

The companies could effect organisational changes such as the establishment of independent profit centres, open offices and India and abroad and implement schemes to train staff and manage retirement, the government said.
For decades, such activities needed permission from bureaucrats in administrative ministries, and often political approval from the cabinet.

To raise debt, the nine chosen companies would no longer require special official decisions. But they must go through routine approvals from the Finance Ministry and the central bank as private companies do, officials said.
The boards will be free to enter joint ventures to acquire technology, or buy or make other arrangements for technology.
The government allowed the nine state companies to decide themselves on setting up financial joint ventures or subsidiaries in India, but stipulated some conditions.
It said the equity of the parent state firm in each such project should not exceed two billion rupees ($55.8 million) or go beyond five percent of the net worth.
The total equity investment of the parent state firm in all joint ventures and subsidiaries together should not exceed 15 percent of its net worth, the statement said. ($1=35.8 rupees)
